Chain-Hop

How well a plain amount-and-time rule pairs a bridge deposit with its withdrawal on the other chain, measured on one window of real traffic.

  • Linking two legs links two transactions. It does not say who sent them or who controls either side.
  • The labels come from the protocols' own transfer IDs, and the matcher never sees them.

Held-out result

Reading the drawing

False candidates pile up on round amounts, and the drawing shows which slider is doing the work.

The grid below has every number the panel shows. These four things are easier to see in the drawing.

  • The traffic never thins.
  • Round amounts are where precision drops. Bridge traffic clusters on round denominations, so the field is bright in horizontal stripes and candidate arcs pile up there: many transfers are exactly $100, while 13.4471 ETH is close to unique. One precision per grid cell hides that it is decent for unusual amounts and poor inside the stripes, which is the case for weighting candidates by how unusual the amount is.
  • Each slider removes different arcs. Tightening the tolerance removes arcs whose ends sit at different heights; tightening the window removes the long, flat ones. The drawing shows which constraint is binding at each setting.
  • A failure has a shape. A sampled deposit with forty candidates draws as a fan. Spread across time, a tighter window would help; stacked at one time and amount, no window will separate them. Hover any particle for its bridge, chain, amount and block time.

Every setting

The settings that catch nearly every labelled pair produce far more candidates than anyone could review.

Each cell is the candidate count over the full window, for one amount tolerance (rows) and time window (columns). Stronger shading means a higher share of the candidates are labelled pairs, on one scale across the table. The strongly shaded cells are also the small ones. Click a cell to move the instrument there.

How the setting was chosen without looking at the test half

Heuristic layers

Requiring a self-transfer raises precision. The destination chain only gives an oracle-informed ceiling.

Amount and time is the baseline. Two layers can sit on top of it: the withdrawal's recipient equals the deposit's sender (self-transfer), or the withdrawal lands on the destination chain named in the deposit event. Each field was audited against the labeller before being scored. Self-transfer passes. The destination chain does not, so its arms appear only as a ceiling and are left out of the headline and the instrument.

Why the destination chain is a ceiling, not a heuristic

Method and reproducibility

Data and labels

Three pulls from Dune, plus a fourth used only for reconciliation. The two leg tables are pulled independently. bridges_evms.flows, the Spellbook's pairing of the two legs on the bridge_transfer_id the protocol emits, is pulled separately and used only to score candidates after they exist. The bake asserts the pairing keys are absent from the payload before writing it.

The matcher, in full
What the metrics measure

Reproducibility checks

A node script (the oracle) runs the same engine source this page runs, and the page re-derives every cell again in your browser. Both refuse any cell that reaches precision and recall of 1.0 together, which would mean the matcher had been handed the answer. That test only catches gross leakage: the destination-chain arms pass it while still leaning on the label. The implementations share one specification, one data pull and one set of labels, so agreement shows the arithmetic is reproducible. It does not show that the method or the labels are right.
